newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: SOCCER-PORTO PRESIDENT HITS OUT AT NEWSPAPER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PORTO PRESIDENT HITS OUT AT NEWSPAPER.

text.p: Porto president Jorge Nuno Pinto da Costa has accused a sports newspaper of mounting a paid campaign against his club.

Pinto da Costa told around 5,000 Porto fans on Saturday that a supporter of the Portuguese champions had offered to supply a story about alleged corruption at the club to Record daily in return for payment. The story was fictional, he said.
Pinto da Costa said the paper had agreed to pay for the story. "There is a paid campaign by Record against Porto," he said.
Pinto da Costa said he would present proof to the police on Monday.
The editor of Record, Rui Cartaxana, declined to comment on the accusations.
Pinto da Costa did not respond to allegations of corruption involving Porto soccer club brought by a Portuguese businessman and Portuguese private television station SIC.

Portuguese soccer has been plunged into crisis by the allegations of attempted match-fixing, with the most serious case involving accusations that Porto sought to bribe a referee ahead of a European match against Aberdeen 12 years ago.
Businessman Fernando Barata has told police that he was asked to approach the Romanian referee in charge of the gameand offer him money to secure a 3-0 win for the Portuguese side in the home leg.
Porto won both legs of the 1984 Cup Winners' Cup semifinal 1-0. Both Porto and the match official have denied any bribery attempt was made.
Porto are also at the centre of another controversy over the payment of a holiday in Brazil for a leading referee in the summer of 1995.
The club has officially admitted that it picked up the 700,000 escudo ($4,600) bill but says that it did so without realising who it was for.
UEFA has demanded a thorough investigation of the various charges and accusations.
Portuguese Federation chairman Gilberto Madail said on Friday he would go to Amsterdam and Zurich next week to brief officials of UEFA and FIFA on the corruption scandals.
Portugal's soccer authorities have pledged to tighten up rules to prevent a recurrence of the scandals rocking the domestic game.
